name: Malar augmentation with fat grafting
lead: Malar augmentation with fat grafting is a cosmetic procedure in which a person's own fat is harvested, usually by liposuction from another body site, processed, and injected into the cheek area to add fullness and projection over the cheekbones.[1] It is a form of autologous soft-tissue augmentation, distinct from cheek implants and from hyaluronic acid fillers. People choose it to get higher, fuller cheeks and a more sculpted midface using their own tissue.

General fat-grafting sources describe facial uses as restoring volume to deflated facial compartments rather than relying only on removing skin, and note that some transferred fat is resorbed over time, so outcomes vary.[1] Fat grafting is often combined with other contouring procedures such as facelifts, chin implants and buccal fat removal.[2]

A 2020 photographic study by Eric Swanson in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open compared 100 facelift patients, 61 of whom also received malar fat injection, and reported about 3 mm of added malar projection that was maintained through follow-up, with calculated fat retention of about 34 percent.[3]

chain: Own fat is harvested and processed

angle.text: Fat injected over the cheekbones adds volume and forward projection to the malar area, giving a fuller, more defined cheek contour. Because it uses the patient's own fat, it is described as an alternative to implants or synthetic fillers.

paras: Fat transfer is generally described as three stages: collecting fat, usually by liposuction; purifying it; and reinjecting it into the target area. It can be done under local or general anesthesia, and sources stress gentle handling and prompt reinjection to help the cells survive.[1]

Facial fat grafting is described as part of a shift from approaches that mainly removed skin and fat toward restoring volume lost in individual facial compartments with age.[1] Applied to the cheeks, the aim is greater fullness or projection in the malar region. Grafting is also used around the eyes, around the mouth, on the hands, in rhinoplasty and for scars.[1]

Swanson's retrospective cohort compared 61 facelift patients who also had malar fat injection with 39 who had a facelift alone, using standardized photographs before surgery and at 1, 3 and 6 months, with 44 patients photographed at 1 year.[3] The fat group gained about 3 mm of projection that was maintained and correlated with the volume injected, while controls had a smaller increase of under 1 mm.[3] Calculated fat retention was around 34 percent.[3]
Overall complication rates in that study were 28 percent, with no significant difference between the fat injection group (32.8 percent) and facelift alone (20.5 percent).[3]

Complications listed for fat grafting in general include swelling, bruising, hematoma, donor-site pain or altered sensation, hypertrophic scarring, infection, contour irregularities, fat necrosis, and injury to underlying structures from the cannula.[1] Transferred fat is said to behave like fat elsewhere in the body, so large weight changes can alter results, and in breast augmentation the body may reabsorb up to half of the graft.[1]

Wikipedia's article on buccal fat extraction notes that removal of the buccal fat pad is often combined with chin liposuction and fat grafting, that it can give an excessively gaunt look as cheeks lose volume with age, and that techniques for restoring buccal fat, including fat injection and dermal fat grafts, are gaining popularity.[2]

A retrospective cohort of 100 facelift patients measured malar projection with and without fat injection, as described above.[3] A separate completed registered trial, NCT05028283 (n=69, started 2021), studied fat grafting for atrophic post-acne scars, a different indication.[4]

Fat grafting is generally discussed alongside implants, fillers and midface surgery as an option for cheek and midface volume. Looksmax.org threads on filling hollows under the eyes and nasolabial folds also discuss topical 'lipofilling' products, a different approach from surgical fat transfer.[5]

timeline.event: Swanson publishes a 100-patient photographic comparison of malar projection with and without fat injection.[3]

card.summary: Your own liposuctioned fat injected into the cheeks for volume; plausible and widely used in the face, but cheek-specific evidence is thin.
card.aka: Autologous fat transfer to the cheeks; lipofilling
card.note: Some grafted fat is resorbed, so results can vary.

quick.overview:
Malar fat grafting uses fat taken from elsewhere on the body, processed and injected into the cheeks to add fullness and projection.

It is discussed as a natural-tissue alternative to implants or fillers. Evidence specific to cheek augmentation is limited in the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: Fat is harvested by liposuction, purified and reinjected into the cheek area; the portion that survives provides lasting volume, and the rest is resorbed.
quick.risks: Reported risks of fat grafting include swelling, bruising, infection, lumpiness or contour irregularity, fat necrosis and unpredictable resorption. It is a medical procedure performed by surgeons.
